description: Somos un equipo de tres estudiantes de secundaria especializados en informática, unidos por nuestra pasión por la tecnología y el desarrollo de soluciones innovadoras. Buscamos constantemente nuevos desafíos que nos permitan poner a prueba nuestras habilidades, aprender, crear y crecer juntos en el mundo de la programación.
summary:
GEODEX is a web application that turns NASA Earth observation data into clear and easy to understand climate trends for 14 countries and 183 regions across the Caribbean, Central America and Mexico. Users search for their country or region on an interactive map and explore monthly data from 2001 to 2025 for temperature, precipitation, soil moisture (NASA POWER), vegetation health (NASA MODIS NDVI via Google Earth Engine) and river discharge (GEOGLOWS).

To act as a true “trend detective,” GEODEX applies the seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope to determine whether each change is statistically significant and how fast it is happening, then projects it to 2030 with a probable range. An AI assistant explains the results in plain Spanish, links peaks to real events such as El Niño, and cites its sources.

This matters because our region is among the most vulnerable to climate change, yet the data that proves it is technical, in English and hard to access. GEODEX makes it usable for students, teachers, farmers and local governments, helping communities understand their changing environment and make informed decisions.
details:
GEODEX is a web application that detects and explains climate trends across 14 countries and 183 regions of the Caribbean, Central America and Mexico. Users search for their country or region on an interactive map, choose a variable and instantly see 25 years of monthly data (2001–2025), a trend line, a projection to 2030 and a plain-language summary of what is happening and what it means for people.

The system works in four stages. First, Python scripts automatically download region boundaries from geoBoundaries and data from three satellite sources: the NASA POWER API for temperature, maximum temperature, precipitation and soil moisture; NASA MODIS (MOD13A3 NDVI), processed in Google Earth Engine, for vegetation health; and GEOGLOWS for river discharge. Each region is averaged over the data cells inside its boundary, and the scripts retry failed downloads, fill short cloud gaps and discard incomplete series. Second, a Flask server applies the seasonal Mann-Kendall test with pymannkendall, which compares each month with the same month in other years, so normal seasonal variation is not mistaken for climate change. It returns the p-value, where p < 0.05 means the trend is significant, and Sen's slope, which shows how fast the variable changes per decade; both are robust to extreme events such as hurricanes. Third, only significant trends are projected to 2030, combining the trend with each month's typical pattern and giving a 95% probable range. Finally, an AI assistant powered by Google Gemini receives the exact computed results and answers questions such as "Why did it happen?" or "What will happen?". It reports real peak values and dates, links them to events such as El Niño through Google Search, explains how variables relate, such as rainfall and river flow, and cites its sources.

The main benefit of GEODEX is that it makes NASA data understandable for people without a scientific background. Colors show whether a change is good or bad for people, and each result explains its real impact on health, water and crops. It is designed for students and teachers who want to learn science with local examples, farmers who need to understand rainfall and drought trends, local governments planning water and disaster preparedness, and journalists and community organizations who need reliable information. Our intended impact is to help communities in one of the most climate-vulnerable regions in the world understand their changing environment and make better decisions.

We built the project with Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS. The backend uses Flask, pymannkendall, NumPy and SciPy, served with Gunicorn and deployed on Render. The frontend uses Leaflet for the interactive map and Plotly for the charts. Data comes from the NASA POWER API, the Google Earth Engine Python API, the GEOGLOWS API and geoBoundaries, and the AI uses the Google Gemini API with Google Search grounding. We also wrote automated tests with unittest and used Git and GitHub for version control.

GEODEX is creative because it combines three satellite sources, so users can see the full chain of how climate affects water and land. Instead of only showing charts, it tells users whether a change is real, how fast it is happening, what it means for people and what could happen next. The AI works as a detective partner that investigates possible causes using real events and verifiable sources, and search works by country or region using local names that people recognize.

Our team considered several key factors. For precision, we used the seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, which are standard methods in climate science, instead of simple averages, and we only project trends that are statistically significant. For data variety and reliability, we combined several official satellite sources to cover more variables and cross-check them, and we validated the data for completeness, physical ranges and agreement with known events, such as the 2023 heat peak during El Niño. We also prioritized accessibility through a Spanish interface, simple explanations and coverage of areas without ground weather stations. We were honest about limitations: river discharge is modeled, satellite data averages large areas and projections assume the trend continues, so GEODEX shows probable ranges and cites its sources. Finally, we considered security and cost by keeping API keys out of the code, limiting AI usage and using only free, open data sources.
